responses.title: How the IR Turret Listens and Acts
story: Picture the turret as a guard dog sitting very still, with its ears pointed at the remote. When the box wakes up, it plugs in its three servos (motors), turns on its IR ear, and moves to a home pose: stopped turning, tilted at 100.

Then it waits. Over and over, many times a second, it asks one question: did a button message just arrive? Each remote button sends its own secret number, called a command code. The top of the sketch gives each number a friendly name, like up or ok.

When a message arrives, the box reads the number and picks the matching action. Left and right turn the whole turret for a short burst, then stop. Up and down tilt it in small steps. OK fires one dart, and star fires all six. Buttons 1 and 2 make it nod yes and shake no.
Every action is built from timing. To turn, the turret starts a motor, waits a set number of milliseconds, then stops it. That is why one press moves it only a little.

steps.label: Name buttons
steps.detail: Each remote button gets a nickname for its secret code number, like ok for 0x1C.

steps.label: Set up
steps.detail: The box attaches the servos to pins 10, 11 and 12, starts the IR ear on pin 9, and goes home.

steps.label: Listen
steps.detail: The loop checks whether a remote message has arrived and decodes it.

steps.label: Get ready again
steps.detail: The resume line tells the IR ear to listen for the next button press.

steps.label: Pick action
steps.detail: The switch compares the code to each button and runs the matching move, like fire() for OK.

steps.label: Timed moves
steps.detail: Turning runs the yaw motor for 150 milliseconds then stops it, while firing runs the roll motor for about 158 milliseconds.

responses.metaphor: The loop is like a guard dog with its ears up, waiting for a whistle, and each button is a different whistle that means a different trick.
responses.watch_for: Press OK and watch the barrel spin one sixth of a turn, then press star and count all six darts go.
